Tumor growth

In one melanoma study, red and near-infrared PBM increased tumor weight and CD31 in mice, with VEGF and signaling changes in cell experiments. The category has no controlled human tumor-growth study; its one human publication is a case report involving combined treatment.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In one melanoma study, red and near-infrared PBM increased tumor weight and CD31 in mice, with VEGF and signaling changes in cell experiments. The category has no controlled human tumor-growth study; its one human publication is a case report involving combined treatment.

Summary of the Evidence

Forty-seven database records represent 47 unique titles. The inventory includes 41 animal-study records, 11 in-vitro records, one human case report, two reviews, one systematic review, and two editorials. Method tags overlap because some papers include both animal and cell experiments. Animal models include mouse, rat, hamster, and unspecified species.

Human and clinical evidence

The only human publication is a case report of combined cancer treatment; it cannot isolate a PBM effect on tumor growth. No controlled patient study was identified. Reviews and editorials do not add patient cohorts.

Animal evidence

Lin and colleagues studied melanoma in mice and cells. The mouse component reported increased tumor weight and CD31, a vascular marker, after red and near-infrared laser exposure. The associated cell work reported changes in VEGF and ERK/p38 signaling. This is a tumor-growth result in a specific model, not a universal effect across cancers or devices (Lin et al. 2023).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Eleven titles include in-vitro experiments. In the Lin paper, cell findings accompany the animal model and are included in the same publication count. The cell experiments examined signaling mechanisms (Lin et al. 2023).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The database describes red and near-infrared low-level laser exposures, but protocols, tumor models, and schedules vary across records. The reported increase occurred in a melanoma model under a specific protocol. The database does not support a single exposure setting or a dose-response conclusion that can be transferred across tumor types.

Interpretation

The evidence is mostly preclinical and mixed across models. The melanoma study's increased tumor weight is a finding that should remain explicit; current records do not determine the direction of PBM's effect on tumor growth in people.

Evidence strength in source summaryTumor growth in animal models: Very low, with mixed direction Human tumor progression: No controlled evidence identified
Publications and records47 database records and 47 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains 47 unique titles, mostly animal and cell studies with different tumor models and exposure schedules. A melanoma mouse-and-cell paper reported increased tumor weight and angiogenesis markers, while the only human report is a combined-treatment case. Replication across models and controlled human evidence are absent.
